document_text:
Verdo Foods - Company and Product Brief

Launch of Proteo Crisps in France. Internal document, prepared for the launch planning team. All

companies, people and figures in this document are fictional and used for demonstration only.

1. Company overview

Verdo Foods S.r.l. is an Italian food company founded in 2020 in Bologna by Giulia Ferri, a food

technologist, and Marco Bassi, former category manager at a large Italian retailer. The company

develops  savoury  snacks  made  from  legumes,  with  a  focus  on  high  protein  content,  short

ingredient lists and sustainable packaging.

In  2024  Verdo  Foods  had  28  employees  and  a  turnover  of  4.2  million  euros,  almost  entirely  in

Italy. Its products are sold in about 2,300 points of sale in Italy (supermarkets, organic shops and

a  selection  of  gyms)  and  through  its  own  online  shop,  which  accounts  for  9%  of  sales.  The

company closed its first profitable year in 2024 and raised a second funding round in early 2025

to finance its first international launch.

Mission: make plant-based protein an everyday snack, not a niche product for athletes or vegans.

2. The product: Proteo Crisps

Proteo  Crisps  are  oven-baked  crisps  made  from  chickpea  flour  and  pea  protein.  They  were

launched in Italy in 2022 and are now the company's best-selling line, with 61% of its turnover.

-    15  g  of  protein  per  40  g  bag,  about  30%  more  than  the  leading  plant-based  protein  crisps  in

Italy.

-    Three  flavours:  Sea  Salt,  Rosemary,  and  Smoked  Paprika.  A  fourth  flavour  (Herbes  de

Provence) is being developed specifically for France.

-  Only six ingredients, no palm oil, no additives; vegan and gluten-free certified.

-  Nutri-Score A for Sea Salt and Rosemary, B for Smoked Paprika.

-  Compostable packaging, introduced in 2024.

-  Shelf life of 9 months, which allows distribution through standard supermarket logistics.

In  Italian  blind  taste  tests  run  by  the  company  in  2024  (420  participants),  Proteo  Crisps  were

preferred to the leading conventional potato crisps by 47% of participants, a tie for 21%, and less

preferred by 32%. Texture was the most appreciated attribute; the Smoked Paprika flavour was

judged too strong by a quarter of participants.

3. Why France, and launch goals

France is the second largest savoury snack market in Europe and the fastest growing market for

protein  snacks  in  Southern  Europe.  French  consumers  are  familiar  with  Nutri-Score,  which  was

created  in  France,  and  the  company  sees  its  Nutri-Score  A  rating  as  a  strong  argument  on  the

shelf.

Goals for the French launch, approved by the board in June 2025:

-  Reach a 2% value share of the French protein snack category within 24 months of launch.

 -  Be listed in at least 1,500 points of sale in the first year.

-  Generate 25% of company turnover from France by the end of 2027.

-  Reach break-even on the French operation in the third year.

The launch is planned for March 2026, starting with the Paris, Lyon and Lille regions.

4. Market context

The figures below come from the NutriMarket Insights report 'Protein snacks in France 2025' and

from the France Snack Panel 2024 consumer survey (both fictional sources for this demo).

In  short,  the  protein  snack  category  is  worth  480  million  euros  and  grows  by  11%  per  year;

plant-based products are 18% of it, and 27% of French adults bought a protein snack in the last

Supermarkets  and  hypermarkets  account  for  68%  of  protein  snack  sales  in  France,  specialised

sport  and  organic  shops  for  17%,  online  for  9%,  and  gyms  and  vending  for  6%  (NutriMarket

Insights 2025).

5. Consumer groups

The  France  Snack  Panel  2024  measured  purchase  intent  for  a  high-protein,  plant-based  crisp

after showing a product concept similar to Proteo Crisps. Group sizes refer to adults aged 18 to

The founders' first instinct is to target vegans, because they show by far the highest enthusiasm

 for the concept and are the most active group on social media. The team has not yet decided on

the target group.

6. Competitive landscape

The main competitors identified by the team in France are:

-  Barebells: protein bars and snacks, strong presence in gyms and supermarkets, sport-oriented

image.

-    Gerble:  French  brand  of  health  and  wellness  foods,  widely  available  in  supermarkets,  with

some protein products.

-  Supermarket private labels, which entered the protein snack category in 2023 with lower prices.

The team has not yet carried out a detailed price comparison of competitors in France.

7. Production and distribution

Proteo Crisps are produced in the company's plant near Bologna, which currently runs at 55% of

its capacity and can supply the French launch without new investment. For France, Verdo Foods

plans  to  work  with  a  national  food  distributor  for  supermarkets  and  to  sell  directly  to  gyms  and

organic  shops  in  the  launch  regions.  The  online  shop  will  be  translated  and  will  ship  to  France

from launch day.

Packaging  will  be  adapted  to  French  labelling  rules,  with  Nutri-Score  shown  on  the  front  of  the

pack.

8. Open points

-  Choice of the target group and of the positioning for France.

-  Launch campaign concept and channel plan.

-  Name of the national distributor (negotiations ongoing with two candidates).

analysis.market_overview: France's savoury snack market was worth 2.9 billion euros in 2024, and the protein snack category 480 million euros [S3]. The protein category grew 11% per year from 2021 to 2024, and plant-based products are 18% of it [S3]. 27% of French adults bought a protein snack in the last three months [S3]. Supermarkets and hypermarkets make up 68% of protein snack sales, specialised sport and organic shops 17%, online 9%, and gyms and vending 6% [S3]. The company calls France the fastest-growing protein snack market in Southern Europe, and sees Nutri-Score, which was created in France, as a shelf argument [S2]. A blog says high-protein food revenue grew more than five-fold between 2020 and 2024, with premium prices 20% to 100% above standard products. It covers all high-protein foods, not only snacks, and is a weak source [S15]. The competitors named by the team are Barebells, Gerblé and private labels [S5]. No reliable shelf-price comparison for protein crisps in French supermarkets is available.

competitors.name: Barebells
competitors.positioning: Protein bars and snacks with a sport-oriented image, strong in gyms and supermarkets [S5]. Bars with 16-20 g of protein and no added sugar [S7]. Sold in France through its own French web shop and, per a Carrefour post, exclusively at Carrefour [S6]. No Barebells crisp was found in France, so it competes through bars.

competitors.name: Gerblé
competitors.positioning: French health and wellness food brand, widely available in supermarkets, with some protein products [S5]. Web results show mainly biscuits and cereal bars, for example Nutri-Score A cocoa-hazelnut bars at Auchan [S9]. It is probably an indirect competitor, with sweet snacks rather than protein crisps. No protein product or price was found. The only prices found are for biscuits, for example 2.39 euros for 250 g of chocolate chip biscuits [S10].

competitors.name: Supermarket private labels
competitors.positioning: Entered the protein snack category in 2023 with lower prices [S5]. Chickpea products exist at Carrefour, such as chickpea crisps for kids, with about 12% of calories from protein, so not a protein positioning [S13]. No private-label protein crisp price was found.

competitors.name: Inlead Protein Chips
competitors.positioning: Protein chips sold in French sports-nutrition online shops, in 6 x 50 g boxes at 12.90 euros [S11]. This is about 2.15 euros per 50 g bag (analyst arithmetic). It is a direct comparable in the sport channel, not a supermarket product.

competitors.name: Gam's Protein
competitors.positioning: Lentil-based protein chips (65 g, Extra Spicy) distributed through the Ankorstore wholesale marketplace [S12]. This points to a specialist or independent retail channel. No price was found.

customer_needs: Great taste is the most important attribute of a protein snack, even among regular users; value, relevance and taste are the main barriers in protein bars [S16]
Texture was the most appreciated attribute of Proteo Crisps in Italian blind tests, while a quarter of participants found Smoked Paprika too strong, so flavour intensity matters [S1]
A clear nutrition signal on the pack: French consumers know Nutri-Score, which was created in France [S2]
Short ingredient lists and less processing: foodwatch France criticises protein products it calls ultra-processed [S14]
Fair price for the protein claim: foodwatch shows protein versions costing nearly double per kg, for example Wasa at Carrefour, 7.09 vs 13.95 euros/kg [S14]
Protein snacks that fit regular physical activity: 71% of French people exercise regularly, per a blog [S15]
Plant-based protein options: plant-based products are 18% of protein snack sales [S3]
Buying in supermarkets: they carry 68% of protein snack sales [S3]

segments.label: Vegans and strict vegetarians
segments.description: The most enthusiastic group, with 72% purchase intent for a high-protein plant-based crisp concept; the most active group on social media [S4]. It is the founders' first instinct, but it is the smallest group.
needs: Short ingredient lists with no additives
Taste that holds up against conventional crisps

segments.label: Weekly sport practitioners
segments.description: The largest group, with 41% purchase intent [S4]. Gyms and vending are 6% of protein snack sales and specialised sport shops are part of a 17% channel with organic shops [S3]. A sports-nutrition survey finds the most regular consumers of sports nutrition products are the most regular sports practitioners (51%), but its sample is unclear [S17].
needs: High protein per portion (15 g per 40 g bag [S1])
Fair price for the protein claim

segments.label: Health-conscious office workers
segments.description: 38% purchase intent [S4]. Overlaps with sport practitioners [S4]. Nutri-Score A on Sea Salt and Rosemary is a relevant argument [S1][S2].
needs: Easy to find in supermarkets or online

segments.label: Parents of school-age children
segments.description: The lowest purchase intent of the four groups, at 22% [S4].
needs: Low-risk, mild flavours (Smoked Paprika judged too strong by a quarter of Italian testers [S1])

data_quality_notes: No product price, marketing budget or distributor is given in the document, and no detailed price comparison was done by the team.

Competitor prices are largely missing: no reliable Barebells unit price in French supermarkets (an Idealo listing shows a 12-pack from 26.16 euros and one offer at 99.95 euros, with no explanation for the gap, so it is unreliable); no price for any Gerblé protein product (biscuit prices only); no price for private-label protein crisps. Barebells, Gerblé and the other brands are therefore set to 'unknown'.
The 'low' price level for private labels comes only from the document's statement that they entered with lower prices [S5]. It has no figures and no web confirmation.

The few protein-crisp prices found (Inlead, around 2.15 euros per 50 g bag, my arithmetic) come from specialist online shops, not supermarkets, which carry 68% of sales. They are a rough indication only. An unbranded 30 g protein crisp at 2.25 euros was found on a diet e-shop and is not listed as a competitor because the brand is not named.

Gerblé and Barebells are not direct crisp competitors on the evidence found: Gerblé shows biscuits and cereal bars, and Barebells shows bars. Gam's Protein and Inlead are direct comparables but were not named in the document.

The market and segment figures (NutriMarket Insights 2025, France Snack Panel 2024) come from the document, are labelled fictional, and could not be checked independently on the web. No web figure conflicts with them.

Segment sizes overlap (for example, many sport practitioners are also office workers), so they cannot be added together. Purchase intent was measured on a concept similar to Proteo Crisps, not on the product itself.
The Italian blind taste test (420 participants) was run by the company in Italy and has not been repeated in France; the Herbes de Provence flavour has not been tested.

Weak or partial web sources: the high-protein foods article is a blog covering mainly dairy and other categories [S15]; the Glanbia page is a supplier's view [S16]; the Nutex survey comes from a sports nutrition brand with an unclear sample [S17]. A Glanbia 2024 five-country study (3,873 respondents) was seen only as a snippet with no figures, so it is not used. Global and unrelated market reports (cheese snacks, premium snacks) were excluded. A GFI Europe item on French plant-based sales (+20.5% over two years) was seen only as a headline and is not used.

The analysts' own arithmetic, not in any source: plant-based protein snacks at 18% of 480M euros is about 86M euros, and a 2% value share is about 9.6M euros. These use 2024 figures, and the category has been growing 11% a year, so check them before using them.

The document states a plan to sell through supermarkets, gyms and organic shops, but the channel plan and national distributor are still open. The channel shares are for the whole category, not Proteo Crisps.

strategy.target_description: French adults aged 18-64 who practise sport every week and want a high-protein, tasty snack they can buy in the supermarket or at the gym, at a fair price for the protein claim.
strategy.positioning_statement: For regular sport practitioners, Proteo Crisps is the high-protein crisp that feels like a real crisp: 15 g of protein per 40 g bag, only six ingredients with no additives, vegan, and Nutri-Score A on Sea Salt and Rosemary. It is positioned as a cleaner, simpler alternative to bar-based protein snacks and to ultra-processed protein products, and as a more credible protein offer than private labels.
strategy.value_proposition: 15 g of plant-based protein in a crisp snack, with a short and clear ingredient list and a Nutri-Score A (Sea Salt, Rosemary), available where sport practitioners already shop.
strategy.pricing_direction: Competitor prices are unknown for Barebells, Gerblé and private-label protein crisps, so no exact price can be justified yet. Direction: price above private labels (described as the low-price option [S5]) to carry the protein claim, but keep the premium moderate, because foodwatch shows protein versions costing nearly double per kg and fair price is a stated need [S14]. The only crisp benchmark is Inlead at about 2.15 euros per 50 g bag in specialist online shops (analyst arithmetic [S11]). It is rough and not a supermarket price. Before fixing the price, run a shelf-price audit in French supermarkets and gyms, and test price acceptance with the target. Use the Inlead benchmark per gram as a ceiling reference, not as a target.
strategy.rationale: SEG2 is the best primary target because it combines the largest size with solid interest. It has 17.5M adults (34% of adults aged 18-64) and 41% purchase intent [S4]. As rough arithmetic of mine (segments overlap, intent was measured on a similar concept, so this is only an order of magnitude), that is about 7M potential buyers. SEG1 (vegans) has the highest intent (72%) but only 1.3M adults, about 0.9M intenders, and plant-based is only 18% of the category [S3][S4]. That is too small for a 2% share and 1,500 points of sale. SEG3 (office workers, 9.0M, 38%) is half the size and overlaps with SEG2 [S4]. SEG4 (parents, 7.1M) has the lowest intent, 22% [S4]. It also needs mild flavours, and Smoked Paprika was judged too strong by a quarter of Italian testers [S1]. Accessibility fits the company goals. Supermarkets carry 68% of protein snack sales, sport and organic shops are part of a 17% channel, and gyms and vending are 6% [S3]. Verdo already sells in supermarkets, organic shops and some gyms in Italy (brief), which suits the 1,500-point goal. SEG2 needs availability in both gyms and supermarkets [S4]. Competition: Barebells is sport-oriented but found only as bars, and per one Carrefour post it is exclusive there [S5][S6][S7]. Gerblé is mostly an indirect competitor with biscuits and cereal bars [S9][S10]. Direct crisp comparables, such as Inlead, sit in specialist online shops [S11]. Claims used are only those not flagged as unverified: 15 g protein per 40 g bag, six ingredients, vegan, Nutri-Score A for Sea Salt and Rosemary (the Nutri-Score is a shelf argument in France [S2]), and short ingredients as a reply to the ultra-processed criticism [S14]. I do not use the '30% more protein than the leading plant-based crisps' claim, because that comparison was made in Italy. I also do not use the Italian taste-test result, because it has not been repeated in France. Lead with Sea Salt and Rosemary, since Smoked Paprika is Nutri-Score B and was judged too strong by some testers. Herbes de Provence has not been tested. Vegan messaging stays as a secondary benefit to reach SEG1 as a bonus audience. Assumptions and risks: the sport-practitioner interest comes from a concept test, not from the product. The Nutex sample is unclear [S17]. Channel shares are for the whole category, not Proteo Crisps. The distributor is not yet chosen, and a possible Barebells exclusivity at Carrefour could limit access there. The marketing budget is unknown, so the Instagram and gym activity should be scaled once it is set.

campaign.concept: Proteo Crisps is the crisp that doesn't make you choose. Built around the moment after training or in the middle of a busy week, the campaign sets a real, crunchy crisp against the "protein snack" that looks like a bar and reads like a chemistry label. We show the facts plainly: 15 g of protein, six ingredients, a Nutri-Score A on Sea Salt and Rosemary. A real crisp, with protein and nothing superfluous.

key_messages.headline: 15 g de protéines. Un vrai croustillant.
key_messages.body: Proteo Crisps : des chips au four, riches en protéines, avec 15 g de protéines par sachet de 40 g. Seulement six ingrédients, sans additifs. Nutri-Score A pour Sea Salt et Rosemary. À retrouver au rayon snacking protéiné.

key_messages.headline: Six ingrédients. Zéro compromis sur le croquant.
key_messages.body: Pois, pois chiche, huile, sel, et c'est tout ou presque : une liste courte et claire, sans huile de palme ni additifs. Végan, sans gluten. Sea Salt et Rosemary : Nutri-Score A.

key_messages.headline: Après l'effort, du croquant.
key_messages.body: 15 g de protéines par sachet de 40 g. Six ingrédients, sans additifs, 100 % végétal. Une chips qui a vraiment du croquant, à glisser dans votre sac de sport. Proteo Crisps : le vrai croustillant. Protéiné.

key_messages.headline: Une recette courte, des protéines végétales.
key_messages.body: Farine de pois chiche et protéine de pois, cuites au four. 15 g de protéines par sachet de 40 g, six ingrédients, sans additifs, végan et sans gluten certifiés. Emballage compostable. Essayez Sea Salt ou Rosemary.

key_messages.headline: Ça, c'est une chips. Et elle a 15 g de protéines.
key_messages.body: Pas une barre, pas une poudre : une vraie chips croustillante, riche en protéines. 6 ingrédients, Nutri-Score A (Sea Salt et Rosemary), végan. Dites-nous votre saveur préférée en commentaire. 👇 #ProteoCrisps

key_messages.headline: Goûtez le croquant protéiné.
key_messages.body: Découvrez Sea Salt, Rosemary et Smoked Paprika : 15 g de protéines par sachet de 40 g, six ingrédients, sans additifs, végan et sans gluten. Commandez votre premier assortiment et livrez-vous à la pause croquante.

content_ideas: Supermarket shelf-ready display and shelf strips in the protein snack aisle, led by Sea Salt and Rosemary, highlighting '15 g de protéines' and Nutri-Score A
Sampling stands in partner gyms during launch month, with sachets handed out at the reception or juice bar
Branded gym poster and locker-room screen series: 'Après l'effort, du croquant' with the 15 g protein and six-ingredient facts
Instagram Reels series 'Le test du croquant': crunch-focused close-ups (ASMR style) filmed in gyms and at home after training, with the ingredient list on screen
Instagram collaborations with French amateur sport practitioners and local gym coaches showing the snack in their gym bag, with clear partnership labelling
Counter display and sampling days in sport and organic shops, with a simple card showing the six ingredients
Own online shop discovery pack with the three flavours and an Instagram-to-shop link, plus a short ingredient-list explainer page
Instagram Stories poll asking the community to react on flavours, including early feedback on the upcoming Herbes de Provence flavour
campaign.visual_direction: Clean, energetic and direct. A bright white or warm off-white base with bold colour blocks per flavour: sea-blue for Sea Salt, herb green for Rosemary, and a warm paprika red for Smoked Paprika. Close-up macro photography of the crisp's crunch and texture, plus real training-bag and locker-room moments, with natural light and no overly muscular stereotypes. Typography is bold, sporty sans-serif with large '15 g' protein callouts. Ingredient list shown openly as a graphic element (six icons). Nutri-Score A logo placed clearly on Sea Salt and Rosemary materials only. Packaging cues: matte, paper-like compostable pack with a large flavour name, a clear 'végan' and 'sans gluten' marker, and a window-style crisp illustration. Gym assets are high-contrast and large-format, while supermarket assets are simple, with a strong shelf-stopping colour band.

issues.message: This need rests on a blog (S15). The analysis itself calls S15 weak and says it covers high-protein foods in general, not snacks. The figure is used to support the sport-practitioner need without any caveat. Drop it. Otherwise replace it with a reliable source, or use the document's own data on weekly sport practitioners (17.5M adults, 41% purchase intent). Evidence: analysis.customer_needs = "71% of French people exercise regularly, per a blog [S15]"

S15 is described in market_overview and data_quality_notes as a blog on the high-protein food market, with revenue growth and price premiums. Nothing in that description supports a figure on how many French people exercise. The 71% looks unsupported by the cited source. Check it against the source or remove it. Evidence: analysis.customer_needs = "71% of French people exercise regularly"

A figure from a sports-nutrition brand's press release with an unclear sample is used in the description of the target segment SEG2. It covers sports nutrition in general, not protein snacks or crisps. Present it only as a weak indication, or remove it, so the segment case rests on the document's panel data. Evidence: analysis.segments[SEG2].description = "the most regular consumers of sports nutrition products are the most regular sports practitioners (51%), but its sample is unclear [S17]"

The exclusive Carrefour distribution of Barebells rests on a single social-media video post. It also contradicts the document, which describes Barebells as strong in gyms and supermarkets. This is a weak source, and the conflict is not listed in data_quality_notes. Flag it as unverified there, or remove 'exclusively'. Evidence: analysis.competitors[Barebells].positioning = "per a Carrefour post, exclusively at Carrefour [S6]"

Inlead is given a price of about 2.15 euros per 50 g bag, yet its price_level is 'unknown'. The Gam's Protein price gap is not named in data_quality_notes either, which only mention other brands in general terms. Set a rough level for Inlead, or explain the inconsistency. List the Gam's missing price explicitly. Evidence: analysis.competitors[Inlead Protein Chips].price_level = ""price_level": "unknown""

The positioning sets Proteo against bars, ultra-processed products and private labels. The analysis names Inlead Protein Chips and Gam's Protein as the direct protein-crisp comparables, and the strategy never says how Proteo differs from them. Private-label chickpea crisps are only about 12% protein calories. 'Short ingredient list, vegan, 15 g protein' is not shown to be unique against the other protein crisps. Add a differentiator against these crisps, such as taste and texture or supermarket availability. Also drop or soften 'more credible than private labels', because no source compares credibility. Evidence: strategy.positioning_statement = "a more credible protein offer than private labels"

The needs the analysis lists for SEG2 (sport practitioners) are high protein per portion, great taste, fair price and availability in gyms and supermarkets. The positioning leads with clean-label, vegan and Nutri-Score arguments. The analysis ties those to SEG3 (office workers) and SEG1 (vegans). Taste and fair price, which are SEG2 needs, are barely addressed. Reorder the positioning around protein, taste and price, and keep clean-label as support. Evidence: strategy.positioning_statement = "only six ingredients with no additives, vegan, and Nutri-Score A"

This item merges two different retail types. Organic shops serve a health or plant-based shopper (SEG1/SEG3), and sport shops serve SEG2. They would need different messages and a different sales approach. Instagram is a media channel, not a distribution channel, and it is listed alongside the shop channels. Separate sport shops from organic shops, or drop organic shops for a sport-practitioner target. Present Instagram as a communication channel. Evidence: strategy.channels = "Sport and organic shops"

The document only says the crisps use chickpea flour and pea protein, with six ingredients in total. It does not list oil or salt as ingredients. This copy names four items and then says "ou presque", so it does not add up to six and it is imprecise on a label-transparency message. Use the actual six-ingredient list from the pack, or drop the list and keep "six ingrédients". Evidence: campaign.key_messages[1].body = "Pois, pois chiche, huile, sel, et c'est tout ou presque"

This sets Proteo against protein bars, which is Barebells' core product. It implies they are chemical and ultra-processed. No input supports this, and it is not tied to the company's own test. The Instagram line "Pas une barre, pas une poudre" follows the same logic. Make it a neutral statement about Proteo's own short ingredient list and do not disparage a product category.
